notes.meaning: God commands Jeremiah to buy a baked clay jar from a potter and gather some leading elders and priests. Earlier, soft clay on a wheel could still be remolded, but this fired jar is set and hard. The leaders must go with him as official witnesses to see God's dramatic message to the nation.

Jeremiah must take the jar outside Jerusalem into the Valley of Hinnom through the Potsherd Gate. That gate led to the city dump where broken pieces of pottery were thrown away. God chooses this unclean valley, known for wicked idol worship, as the place to speak His judgment.

Jeremiah addresses both the royal leaders and the ordinary citizens with the Lord's message. God warns that He is about to send a disaster so shocking that it will make the ears of anyone who hears of it ring. The sudden ruin would leave the entire nation completely stunned.

The Lord explains the reasons for this severe judgment. The people had forsaken Him, treating His holy city like a pagan, foreign place. They worshiped strange idols and filled the land with the murder of innocent people.

The people had built altars to the false god Baal and burned their own children as sacrifices. God declares that He never commanded, spoke of, or desired such horrible wickedness. True worship of the Lord can never include deeds that violate His holy nature.

differ.view: Reformed teachers see God's words that He did not command this as a foundation for worship: whatever God has not commanded in His word is forbidden.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Many Christians apply this passage to modern abortion, teaching that God treasures child life from conception and deeply hates the killing of the unborn.

notes.meaning: The valley was called Topheth, a name linked to beating drums to drown out the screams of sacrificed children. God announces that it will receive a new name: the Valley of Slaughter. Soon it will be filled with the dead bodies of the unfaithful people themselves.

God announces that He will completely pour out and ruin all the survival plans of Judah's leaders. Their armies will fall by the sword before their enemies in that very valley. So many will die that their corpses will be left unburied as food for vultures and wild beasts.

Jerusalem will become a barren ruin and an object of mockery. Travelers passing through will be appalled at its total destruction and will scoff at its wounds. Sin had turned the glorious city into a public disgrace.

During the long enemy siege, food will run out completely. Starvation will become so terrible that trapped families will eat the flesh of their own sons and daughters, and neighbors will turn on each other. This horrible suffering fulfilled the exact curses warned about in the law of Moses.

Jeremiah must smash the clay jar right before the eyes of the priests and elders. This dramatic action proved that the coming disaster was real and unstoppable. Unlike soft clay, a hardened jar cannot be remolded once it is broken.

God explains that He will break the city and the nation just like that clay jar, leaving it beyond human repair. The destruction by the invading army would be total. The dead will be buried in Topheth until no empty ground is left.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the phrase about burying until there is no room is missing in the earliest Greek manuscripts and was likely added here from chapter 7.

notes.meaning: The Lord declares that the entire city of Jerusalem will end up just like Topheth. It will become an unclean place filled with corpses and rubble. The once-holy city would be treated as an open burial pit.

All the houses of Jerusalem, including the royal palaces, will be completely defiled. The people had used their flat rooftops as altars to burn incense to the sun, moon, and stars, and to pour drink offerings to idols. Because false worship was practiced in every home, judgment would strike every home.

Jeremiah finishes his task in the valley and returns to the temple. He stands in the large public courtyard where the crowds gathered. There he prepares to proclaim the same warning to the common people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that this closing scene was drawn from a historical account written by Jeremiah's scribe Baruch, because Jeremiah is spoken of in the third person.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah warns that God will bring every promised disaster on the city and its surrounding towns. This ruin is coming because the people acted like stubborn oxen and stiffened their necks against God's word. Their refusal to listen brought about their own downfall.
